emergency_call.heading: Calling 911
lines: In an emergency, dial 911 from your phone immediately.
An emergency is any situation that requires immediate assistance from the police, fire department or ambulance.
When you call 911, be prepared to answer the call-taker's questions, which may include:
The location of the emergency, including the street address
The phone number you are calling from
The nature of the emergency

Details about the emergency, such as a physical description of a person who may have committed a crime, a description of any fire that may be burning, or a description of injuries or symptoms being experienced by a person having a medical emergency

Remember, the call-taker's questions are important to get the right kind of help to you quickly. Be prepared to follow any instructions the call-taker gives you. Many 911 centers can tell you exactly what to do until help arrives, such as providing step-by-step instructions to aid someone who is choking or needs first aid or CPR. Do not hang up until the call-taker instructs you to do so.

emergency_call.heading: Can I text 911 for emergency assistance?
lines: Calling 911 by sending a text message is increasing across the United States, and efforts are underway to receive text messages at call centers nationwide. If you need emergency assistance, it is always best to call 911 if you can, and text if you can’t.

Even if text-to-911 services are available in your community, a voice call remains the best way to reach 911. If you send a text message to 911, but text-to-911 services are not available in your community, you should receive an immediate bounce-back message from the wireless provider telling you that the text message was not delivered. For more information about text-to-911, go to the Federal Communications Communications “Text to 911: What You Need to Know” page.

bleeding.heading: Application of Direct Pressure
lines: Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is difficult to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding, or while moving the casualty. While packing a wound, maintain constant, direct pressure, at the source of the bleeding to be effective.

bleeding.heading: Application of Tourniquets
lines: 4-39. A hasty TQ is implemented as "high and tight" on the wounded extremity or when the bleeding source is ambiguous during the CUF phase. However, during TFC, all TQs should be deliberate, placed two to three inches above the wound directly on the skin, not over clothing. Once the casualty is in a safer position, the bleeding source should be reassessed, and the effectiveness of the TQs verified. If bleeding remains uncontrolled, a second TQ may be necessary, particularly for severe bleeding wounds of the thigh.

4-40. It is crucial to recognize that TQs should be used cautiously, with the optimal safe duration being less than two hours. Beyond this timeframe, tissues may start to die, potentially leading to limb loss after six hours. Regular reassessment of TQ effectiveness is necessary, including checking for stopped bleeding, absent distal pulse, and ensuring no pulse below the TQ on the limb. Common errors when applying TQs include not using one, when necessary, not tightening it adequately, and using it for minimal bleeding. Additionally, TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care. If the source of massive bleeding is evident, such as from an amputation or major wound, immediate bleeding control measures like applying a TQ or wound packing should be initiated, especially in areas where a TQ cannot be used, such as the groin, armpit, or neck. The following steps address tourniquet application in CUF for all Service Members, CLS, and medical personnel.
4-41. One-Handed (Windlass) TQ Application CUF:
Remove TQ from JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the self-adhering band.
Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
Ensure that all the slack in the self-adhering band is pulled through the routing buckle before the band is fastened back on itself and the windlass is twisted.
Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip.
Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips.
Secure the windlass safety strap.
If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover.
Note. Do not document the TQ application time until the TFC phase.

bleeding.heading: Expedient Techniques for Hemorrhage Control
lines: 4-79. Using one of the CoTCCC-recommended TQs is the safe and preferred procedure for hemorrhage control. Improvised TQs are much less effective than commercially available TQs discussed in paragraph 4-37 on page 48. Improvised TQs are difficult to make and apply without extensive practice, however they may be needed in situations where commercially produced TQs are unavailable, or supplies have been exhausted.
CAUTION The risks associated with using improvised TQs include:
Damage may occur to the skin if the band is too narrow.
Bleeding may worsen.
Bleeding may not be completely controlled.
Likely to loosen overtime from not being properly secured.

4-80. If a TQ is not available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the source of the heaviest bleed, FIRST. If this fails to control the bleeding in an arm or leg, only then consider an alternate improvised TQ.

4-81. An alternate improvised TQ uses other materials on hand. In constructing one, it is recommended that you fold a cravat (or other pliable material) to a width of approximately 1 ½ to 2 inches and tighten it with some sort of windlass rod (a straight rod that can be used to twist the material tighter). Then secure the rod to ensure it does not loosen.

Note. The cravat is included in the JFAK, however it is not part of the Army IFAK Generation 1 or 2. To resource the cravat for the Army IFAK, the nomenclature is: Sterile Burn Dressing Cravat, NSN: 6510-01-587-6579; Muslin Compressed Bandage NSN: 6510-00-201-1755.

4-82. An improvised TQ should not be used except as an absolute last resort when there is no other option to control life-threatening bleeding. If no TQ is available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the main source of bleeding.
4-83. Continue to check the TQ, as improvised TQs are prone to loosening due to (but not limited to) casualty movement, shifting fluid, and quality of improvised material.

bleeding.heading: Application of Wound Packing
lines: 4-67. Wounds should not be blindly packed. Effort must be taken to locate the source of bleeding and apply direct pressure immediately while preparing the gauze.
4-68. Wound packing:
Identify and expose the wound.
Locate the source of the most active bleeding and apply direct pressure, while preparing the hemostatic dressing.
Remove the hemostatic dressing from its sterile package and pack it into the wound tightly, directly over the site of the most active bleeding.
Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound.
Ensure the hemostatic dressing extends one to two inches above the skin.
Hold continuous direct pressure for a minimum of three minutes.
Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped.
Apply a pressure bandage over the hemostatic dressing to secure it in place.
Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped. If blood is seeping through or around the hemostatic dressing, the bleeding is not controlled, and the following steps should be applied:
If extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove the initial, ineffective hemostatic dressing and replace them with new hemostatic dressings.
If extra hemostatic dressings are unavailable, leave initial, ineffective hemostatic dressing in place and add extra gauze over the wound tract.

If roller or compressed gauze was used initially, due to unavailability of hemostatic dressings, leave initial, ineffective roller or compressed gauze in place and add extra gauze over the wound tract.
Once bleeding has been controlled, apply a pressure bandage over the wound packing material to secure it in place.
Note. More than one hemostatic dressing may be required to stop the blood flow.

not_breathing.heading: External chest compressions
lines: A general outline of the steps involved in conducting external chest compressions is:
Position: Ensure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface, such as the ground or a CPR board. Kneel beside the person's chest.
Hand Placement: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest, between the nipples. For infants or children, use two or three fingers instead of the entire hand.

Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two inches (five centimeters) deep. For infants or children, compress the chest about one-third to one-half of its depth.
Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This equates to about two compressions per second.
Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood.

Compression to Ventilation Ratio: If you are performing CPR alone, do cycles of 30 chest compressions to two rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask). If there are two rescuers, the ratio can be 30:2 or continuous chest compressions with ventilation being delivered by the other rescuer.
Continue until Help Arrives: Keep performing chest compressions until professional medical help arrives, or until the person shows signs of movement or starts breathing.

not_breathing.heading: Signs and symptoms
lines: A person may be in cardiac arrest if they:
Collapse suddenly and lose consciousness (pass out).
Are not breathing or are gasping for air.
Don't respond to shouting or shaking.
Don't have a pulse.
If you believe someone is having a cardiac arrest, call 9-1-1 right away, look for an automated external defibrillator (AED), and give CPR until medical professionals arrive.

not_breathing.heading: Duration of CPR
lines: 6-47. The duration of CPR can vary depending on the circumstances and response of the individual being treated. In general, CPR should be continued until one of the following conditions is met:
Signs of Life: If the person shows obvious signs of life, such as breathing normally, coughing, or moving, CPR can be stopped.
Professional Medical Help Arrives: CPR should be continued until professional medical personnel take over the resuscitation efforts.
Provider Fatigue: If the person performing CPR becomes too exhausted to continue effectively, they can switch with another trained individual to maintain the quality of compression.

choking.heading: Opening the Obstructed Airway: Conscious Casualty
choking.scope: Clearing an airway obstruction in a conscious casualty can be managed while they are either standing or sitting.
lines: 5-29. Clearing an airway obstruction in a conscious casualty can be managed while they are either standing or sitting. However, it's critical to recognize that an obstructed airway can lead to oxygen deficiency in the brain, resulting in respiratory arrest, unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death.

5-30. To assess and manage airway obstruction, start by asking the casualty if they can speak or if they are choking. Additionally, check for the universal choking sign (see figure 5-11 on page 67). If the casualty can speak or cough effectively, encourage them to continue coughing. This indicates that they still have good air exchange, and you should not interfere with their efforts to expel the obstruction.

5-31. However, if you notice high-pitched sounds when the casualty breathes or coughs, indicating poor air exchange, or if the casualty is unable to breathe, immediate action is required. Call for help and prepare to perform manual thrusts to clear the obstruction. Use abdominal thrusts, also known as the Heimlich maneuver, by positioning your hands between the waist and the rib cage and delivering quick upward thrusts. For individuals in advanced stages of pregnancy, those who are markedly obese, or if there is a significant abdominal wound, use chest thrust instead. This involves placing your hands in the center of the breastbone and pushing sharply inward and upward.

choking.heading: Infants (babies under 1 year-old)
lines: First aid for choking infants alternates a cycle of special back blows (five back slaps) followed by special chest thrusts (five adapted chest compressions). In the back blows maneuver, the rescuer slaps on the baby's back. It is recommended that the baby receive them being slightly leaned upside-down on an inclination. There exist several ways to achieve this:

According to a widely propagated modality: the rescuer sits down on a seat with the baby, and supports the baby with a forearm and its respective hand. The baby's head must be carefully held with that hand (approximately by the face), and kept in a normal position, facing forward, not inclinated. Then the baby's body can be leaned forward upside-down along the rescuer's thighs, and receive the slaps.

In the chest thrusts manoeuver, the baby's body is placed lying face up on a surface (it can be the rescuer's thighs, lap or forearm). Then, the rescuer does the compressions pressing with only two fingers on the lower half of the bone that is along the middle of the chest from the neck to the belly (on the chest bone, named sternum, on its part that is the nearest to the belly). Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in children less than one year old because they can cause liver damage.
The back blows and chest thrusts are alternated in cycles of five back blows and five chest compressions until the object comes out of the infant's airway or until the infant becomes unconscious.
If choking is unresolved despite these rescue attempts, it is vital that somebody calls to the emergency medical services and continue first aid until they arrive.

choking.heading: Apply Abdominal Thrusts
lines: 5-33. Prior to applying abdominal thrust, first responders should administer five back blows. Abdominal thrust can be accomplished by using the following procedures: •
Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their waist.

Make a fist with one hand and grasp it with the other. The thumb side of your fist should be against the casualty’s abdomen, in the midline and slightly above the casualty’s navel, but well below the tip of the breastbone (figure 5-12 on page 68).
Press the fists into the abdomen with a quick backward and upward thrust (figure 5-13 on page 68).
Each thrust should be a separate and distinct movement.
Continue performing abdominal thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive.
If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with the steps to open the airway.

heart_attack.heading: Symptoms
heart_attack.locator: Symptoms; Call 9-1-1 if you notice symptoms of a heart attack
lines: The major symptoms of a heart attack are:

Chest pain or discomfort. Most heart attacks involve discomfort in the center or left side of the chest that lasts for more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back. The discomfort can feel like uncomfortable pressure, squeezing, fullness, or pain.
Feeling weak, light-headed, or faint. You may also break into a cold sweat.
Pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck, or back.
Pain or discomfort in one or both arms or shoulders.
Shortness of breath. This often comes along with chest discomfort, but shortness of breath also can happen before chest discomfort.
Other symptoms of a heart attack could include unusual or unexplained tiredness and nausea or vomiting. Women are more likely to have these other symptoms. Learn more about women and heart disease.
Call 9-1-1 if you notice symptoms of a heart attack

If you notice the symptoms of a heart attack in yourself or someone else, call 9-1-1 immediately. The sooner you get to an emergency room, the sooner you can get treatment to reduce the amount of damage to the heart muscle. At the hospital, health care professionals can run tests to find out if a heart attack is happening and can decide the best treatment.

In some cases, a heart attack requires cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or an electrical shock (defibrillation) to the heart to get the heart pumping again. Bystanders trained to use CPR or a defibrillator may be able to help until emergency medical personnel arrive.
Remember, the chances of surviving a heart attack are better the sooner emergency treatment begins.

shock.heading: Prevention of Shock
lines: 7-8. It is more effective to prevent shock through hemorrhage control than to treat it once it has developed. Even in cases where shock is already present, the most critical first action is to control any bleeding. Continuously reassess all bleeding control measures, such as tourniquets and pressure dressings, to ensure they remain effective and are adjusted tightly as soon as possible. This is a crucial step in treating shock.

shock.heading: Position the Casualty for Shock
lines: 7-13. Control bleeding and then take steps to prevent shock by elevating the casualty’s legs higher than the casualty's heart if their airway tolerates lying flat on their back.
7-14. Conduct a bleeding re-check by:
Reassess every TQ and dressing that may have been applied earlier.
Expose the area and determine if bleeding is controlled.
Expose and clearly mark all TQ sites with the time of TQ application if not previously done.
When time and the tactical situation permit, check for further bleeding, and for pulses further out on the limb than the TQ.

7-15. Move the casualty under a permanent or improvised shelter to shade them from direct sunlight. If the casualty is conscious, place the casualty in the shock recovery position (see figure 7-1), which is on their back with their feet elevated slightly above the level of their heart. This will help their blood circulation. A log, field pack, box, rolled field jacket, or other stable objects can be used to elevate their feet. If a sitting position makes it easier for the casualty to breathe, that is fine.
7-16. The following steps will also significantly help in the prevention of shock:
Loosen clothing at the neck, waist, or anywhere is binding.
WARNING Do not loosen clothing if in a chemically contaminated area.
Prevent the casualty from getting chilled or overheated. Using a blanket or clothing, cover the casualty to avoid loss of body heat by wrapping the blanket completely around the casualty.
Note. Ensure no part of the casualty is touching the ground, as this increases loss of body heat.
Calm and reassure the casualty by— ▪ Taking charge and showing self-confidence. ▪ Assuring the casualty that they are being taken care of.
Watch the casualty closely for life-threatening conditions and check for other injuries, if necessary.
Seek medical aid.
Record the treatment on DD Form 1380.
WARNING If the casualty has a fractured lower extremity, do not place the casualty in the shock position until the fracture has been splinted.

7-17. When providing first aid for shock, DO NOT give the casualty any food or drink. If you must leave the casualty or if they are unconscious, turn their head to the side (see figure 7-2) to prevent them from choking, if they vomit.

recovery_position.heading: Check responsiveness and the recovery position
lines: 5-10. Check for responsiveness (figure 5-2 step A on page 61) and establish whether the casualty is conscious by gently shaking them and asking, “Are you OK?” Call for help (figure 5-2 step B on page 61) and then position the unconscious casualty so that they are lying in the recovery position, head tilted back; chin away from chest (figure 5-2 step C on page 61) by —
Straightening the casualty’s legs.
Moving the casualty’s arm that is nearest to you. Move it so that it is straight and above their head. Repeat the procedure for the other arm placing it by their side.
Kneeling beside the casualty with your knees near their shoulders (leave space to roll their body).
Placing one hand behind their head and neck for support. On your other hand, grasp the casualty under their arm (figure 5-2 step C on page 61).
Rolling the casualty towards you using a steady, even pull. The casualty’s head and neck should stay in line with their back.

5-11. The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty’s nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. However, if a neck injury is suspected and the jaw-thrust technique will be used, kneel at the casualty’s head, looking towards their feet.

WARNING If the casualty is lying on their chest (prone position), cautiously roll the casualty as a unit so that their body does not twist. The twisting may further complicate a back, neck, or spinal injury.

recovery_position.heading: Recovery position
lines: 5-24. The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty’s nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. The recovery position also helps to protect against inhaling vomit if the casualty throws up. If a casualty can breathe on their own, let them assume the best position (position of comfort) that allows them to breathe, including sitting up.

cold.heading: Hypothermia
lines: Hypothermia is an unusually low body temperature. A temperature below 95 degrees is an emergency.
Signs: Shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech or drowsiness.
Actions: Go to a warm room. Warm the center of the body first—chest, neck, head and groin. Keep dry and wrapped up in warm blankets, including the head and neck.

cold.heading: First Aid for Hypothermia
lines: 8-8. The goals for first aid for hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. If untreated, hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Evacuate as soon as possible with the casualty lying down.
CAUTION Do not allow the casualty to use tobacco, consume alcohol, or caffeinated drinks.
8-9. Re-warming techniques include—
Remove the casualty from the cold environment.
Replace wet clothing with dry clothing.
Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket.
Wrap the casualty from head to toe.
Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty.
If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids.
Seek medical aid.

8-10. Hypothermia is a serious condition that requires professional evaluation and treatment. Attempting to rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals using appropriate techniques. While waiting for help to arrive, focus on preventing further heat loss and providing support to the person.

cold.heading: Hypothermia and afterdrop
lines: 17-30. The risks differ with environmental hypothermia. Victims of moderate to severe environmental hypothermia are known to have a risk of an irregular heartbeat associated with “afterdrop.” Afterdrop is the continued fall of deep body temperatures during rewarming after hypothermia. Afterdrop is thought to endanger the heart by further cooling from cold blood presumed to be returning to the body’s center or core.

17-31. Environmental hypothermic casualties should be monitored and gently handled as afterdrop is not always observed. The goals for overall casualty treatment (such as hemorrhage control and resuscitation in TCCC versus warming measures along with gentle handling in environmental hypothermia) should be understood, trained, and rehearsed. For further discussion on hypothermia see Chapter 8.

cold.heading: Frostbite
lines: Frostbite causes loss of feeling and color around the face, fingers and toes.
Signs: Numbness, white or grayish-yellow skin, firm or waxy skin.
Actions: Go to a warm room. Soak in warm water. Use body heat to warm. Do not massage or use a heating pad.

cold.heading: Frostbite
lines: 17-24. Frostbite is a cold weather injury that occurs when tissues freeze due to prolonged exposure to extreme cold temperatures. It typically affects extremities, such as the fingers, toes, ears, and nose, but can also occur in other exposed areas of the body. The signs and symptoms of frostbite may vary depending on the severity, and they can include:
Cold, pale, or bluish skin.
Numbness or a loss of sensation in the affected area.
Tingling or a “pins and needles” sensation.
Hard or waxy appearance of the skin.
Swelling or blistering (in severe cases).
Pain or a burning sensation (as the affected area rewarms).
Blackened or gangrenous tissue (in severe, untreated cases).
17-25. If someone is suspected of having frostbite, it is important to provide immediate first aid and seek medical attention. Take the following first aid steps:
Move to a warm environment: Get the person out of the cold and into a warm area as soon as possible to prevent further damage.
Remove wet or constrictive clothing: Take off any wet clothing or accessories that could contribute to heat loss or restrict blood flow to the affected area.

Gradually rewarm the affected area: Immerse the frostbit area in warm (not hot) water or use warm compresses. Avoid using direct heat sources like fires or heating pads, as the person may not be able to sense heat properly and could burn the skin.
Avoid rubbing or massaging the area: Vigorous rubbing can further damage the tissues. Let the affected area rewarm naturally.
Protect and elevate the affected area: Once the frostbitten area has thawed, cover it with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. Keep the area elevated to reduce swelling, if possible.

Offer pain relief if needed: Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. However, consult a health care professional before administering any medication.

Seek medical attention: Frostbite requires medical evaluation and treatment. Even if the frostbite appears mild, professional medical care is essential to assess the extent of the injury and prevent complications.
17-26. Frostbite can cause long-term damage, including tissue loss and nerve damage. Prompt and appropriate treatment is crucial for minimizing complications and maximizing recovery.

cold.heading: First Aid for Frostbite
lines: CAUTION Avoid thawing the affected area if it is possible that the injury may refreeze before reaching the medical treatment facility.
12-12. First aid measures for frostbite include—
Local rewarming at room temperature or using body heat.
Loosen or remove constricting clothing and remove jewelry.
CAUTION DO NOT massage the skin or rub anything on the frozen parts.
Move the casualty to a sheltered area, if possible.
Protect the affected area from further cold or trauma.
Once a tissue is thawed, it must not freeze again. If there is the possibility of tissue refreezing, it is better not to thaw it in order to avoid damaging tissue further.
Avoid exposure to excessive heat (open flame, stove tops, steam, heat packs) or rubbing affected tissue.

All Soldiers with a peripheral freezing injury must be suspected of being hypothermic and treated appropriately. During field management, it is more important to prevent hypothermia than to rewarm frostbite rapidly.
Seek medical aid.
Evacuate the casualty.

burns.heading: Home Fires: clothes on fire
lines: If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll – stop immediately, drop to the ground and cover your face with your hands. Roll over and over or back and forth until the fire is out. If you or someone else cannot stop, drop and roll, smother the flames with a blanket or towel. Use cool water to treat the burn immediately for three to five minutes. Cover with a clean, dry cloth. Get medical help right away by calling 9-1-1 or the fire department.

burns.heading: Burn Care
lines: 12-9. Burn care in TCCC is very basic. Eliminating the source of the burn should be the initial priority. Providing any treatment prior to removing the casualty from the source of the burn or extinguishing the cause of the burn will be ineffective and harmful to the casualty and casualty response personnel.
12-10. Electrical burn care consists of—
Eliminating the source of electrical burns.
Turning off any sources of electricity that have been exposed to the casualty (if applicable).
Using nonconductive material to drag the casualty away from the electrical source (if it cannot be turned off).
Note. Types of nonconductive material include rope, clothing, and dry wood.
Moving the casualty to a safe place.

WARNING Do not touch the casualty or the electrical source with your bare hands. You will be injured too! High voltage electrical burns from an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).
12-11. Thermal burn care consists of—
Stopping the source of the thermal burn and remove the casualty from the source of the burn.
Extinguishing any flames on the casualty, cut the clothing around the burned area, and gently lift away.
CAUTION If clothing is stuck to the burn, ensure you cut around the clothing and leave the stuck clothing in place.
Avoid grabbing the burned area while moving or picking up the casualty.

burns.heading: Chemical Burn Care
lines: 12-12. Chemical burn care consists of—
Eliminating the source of chemical burns.
Brushing off dry chemicals (carefully) with a clean, dry cloth.
Flush the burned area with copious amounts of flowing water to remove any liquid chemicals.
Applying a wet barrier (water-soaked gauze, clothing, or mud) with an occlusive dressing.
Advising medical personnel immediately.
WARNING Do not submerge a chemical burn casualty in water. This will greatly contribute to hypothermia and spread the irritation.
12-13. All burn care consists of—
Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions.
Checking for additional injuries.
Treating for shock (if applicable).
Seeking medical aid.
Annotating all treatment and care on DD Form 1380.

heat.heading: Heat-Related Illnesses
heat.locator: Heat stroke, heat cramps, heat exhaustion
lines: Know the signs of heat-related illnesses and ways to respond. If you are sick and need medical attention, contact your healthcare provider for advice and shelter in place if you can. If you are experiencing a medical emergency call 9-1-1.
Get more detailed information about heat-related illnesses from the CDC and National Weather Service.
HEAT STROKE
Signs:
Extremely high body temperature (above 103 degrees F)
Red, hot and dry skin with no sweat
Rapid, strong pulse
Dizziness, confusion or unconsciousness

If you suspect heat stroke, call 9-1-1 or take the person to a hospital immediately. If possible, move the person suffering from heat stroke into a cool, shaded area. Remove any outer clothing. Place a cold, wet cloth or ice pack on the head, neck, armpits, and groin. Alternatively, soak the person’s clothing with cool water. Elevate their feet.
HEAT CRAMPS
Signs: Muscle pains or spasms in the stomach, arms or legs
HEAT EXHAUSTION
Signs: Heavy sweating, paleness, muscle cramps, tiredness, weakness, fast or weak pulse, dizziness, headache, fainting, nausea, vomiting

If you have signs of heat cramps or heat exhaustion, go to a cooler location and cool down by removing excess clothing and taking sips of sports drinks or water. Call your healthcare provider if symptoms get worse or last more than an hour.

heat.heading: Heat Stroke
lines: 17-14. Heat stroke is a severe and potentially life-threatening illness characterized by a rapid increase in body temperature. It occurs when the body's cooling mechanisms fail to regulate internal heat, often because of prolonged exposure to high temperatures or physical exertion in hot environments. Heat stroke is a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention. The signs and symptoms of heat stroke may include:
Altered mental state or confusion.
Headache, dizziness, or fainting.
Nausea or vomiting.
Difficulty breathing.
Hot, dry skin (lack of sweating).
High body temperature (typically above 104°Fahrenheit or 40°Celsius).
Rapid and strong heartbeat.
Seizures.
17-15. If someone is suspected of having heat stroke, it is crucial to seek emergency medical help immediately. While waiting for medical professionals to arrive, follow these first aid steps:
Move the person to a cooler location: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned area as quickly as possible.
Call for emergency assistance: Dial 911 or the appropriate local emergency number to request immediate medical help to include MEDEVAC.

Cool the person rapidly: Reduce their body temperature as quickly as possible. You can immerse the person in a tub of cold water, use ice cooling sheets or apply cold water to their body using wet towels or sponges. Fan the person while misting them with cool water to enhance cooling.

Monitor their vital signs: Keep a close eye on the person's breathing, pulse, and level of consciousness. If they stop breathing and you can no longer find a pulse, begin CPR if you are trained to do so.

17-16. It's important to note that heat stroke is a severe condition, and professional medical treatment is essential. Rapid cooling of the body is crucial in preventing potential organ damage and reducing the risk of complications.

heat.heading: Heat Exhaustion
lines: 17-9. Heat exhaustion is a heat-related condition that occurs when the body becomes overheated due to prolonged exposure to high temperatures and inadequate fluid replacement. It is considered a milder form of heat illness compared to heat stroke. Signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion may include:
Heavy sweating.
Weaknesses and fatigue.
Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Headache.
Nausea or vomiting.
Pale, cool, or clammy skin.
Rapid and shallow breathing.
Elevated heart rate.
Muscle cramps.
Feeling faint or fainting.
17-10. If a Service member is suspected to have heat exhaustion, immediate first aid treatment should be provided. The first aid steps to treat heat exhaustion are:
Move the Service member to a cooler environment: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned area.

Encourage rest and rehydration: Have the Service member lie down and elevate their legs slightly. Provide them with cool water and or an electrolyte-containing sports drink to sip on. Avoid alcohol or caffeine.

Cool the Service member's body: Loosen or remove any tight or unnecessary clothing. Apply a cool, wet cloth or towels to their skin, especially on the neck, face, and armpits. Use a fan or create air movement to aid in evaporation.
Monitor their condition: Stay with the Service member and observe their symptoms. If they do not improve within 30 minutes or their condition worsens, seek medical assistance immediately.

17-11. Heat exhaustion can progress to heat stroke, a life-threatening condition. If the person's symptoms worsen, they become disoriented, confused, or lose consciousness, immediately call for medical assistance.

broken_bone.heading: Apply the splint
lines: 13-34. Apply the splint in place by—
Splinting the fracture in the position found. DO NOT attempt to reposition or straighten the injury. If it is an open fracture, stop the bleeding and protect the wound.
Covering all wounds with field dressings before applying a splint. Remember to use the casualty’s field dressing, before using your own.
Placing one splint on each side of the fracture. Make sure that the splints reach, if possible, beyond the joints above and below the fracture.

Tying the splints by— ▪ Securing each splint in place above and below the fracture site with cravats, or improvised material. Improvised materials, such as gauze bandage, strips of cloth, belts, or whatever other materials you have, may be used. ▪ With minimal motion to the injured areas, place and tie the splints with the bandages. ▪ Push splint material through and under the natural body curvatures, and then gently position splint material, and tie in place. ▪ Using square knots. Tie all knots on the splint away from the casualty (figure 13-3). DO NOT tie knots directly over the suspected fracture site.
13-35. Check the splint for tightness—
CHECK to ensure that the bandages are tight enough to securely hold splinting materials in place, but not so tight that circulation is impaired.

RECHECK the circulation after application of the splint. Check the skin color and temperature. This is to ensure that the bandages holding the splint in place have not been tied too tightly. A fingertip check can be made by inserting the tip of the finger between the bandaged knot and the skin.
MAKE any necessary adjustments without allowing the splint to become ineffective.

broken_bone.heading: Improvised splints, padding and bandages
lines: 13-22. Splints may be improvised from such items such as boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs, or cardboard. If nothing is available for a splint, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a fractured arm, and the uninjured leg can be used to immobilize (to some extent) the fractured leg.

13-23. Padding may be improvised from such items as a jacket, blanket, poncho, shelter half, or leafy vegetation. Padding when splinting a fracture is essential for the well-being of the casualty. It promotes comfort, even pressure distribution, stability, protection against skin issues, and helps manage swelling, all of which contributes to an effective and safer management of fractures, especially in situations where immediate medical care may not be readily available.

13-24. Bandages may be improvised from belts, rifle slings, handkerchiefs, or strips torn from clothing, or blankets. Narrow materials such as wire, or cord should not be used to secure a splint in place. The application of wire or narrow material to an extremity could cause tissue damage and a TQ effect.

13-25. A sling is a bandage suspended from the neck to support an upper extremity. If a bandage is not available, a sling can be improvised by using the tail of a coat, shirt, or pieces of cloth torn from such items as clothing and blankets. The cravat is ideal for this purpose. Remember that the casualty’s hand should be higher than their elbow, and their fingers should be always showing. The sling should be applied so that the supporting pressure is on the uninjured side.

13-26. Swathes are any bands (pieces of cloth or straps) that are used to further immobilize a splinted fracture. Cravats are often used and are called swathe bandages. The purpose of the swathe is to immobilize; therefore, the swathe bandage is placed above or below the fracture, not on top of the fracture.

broken_bone.heading: Cautions when splinting
lines: 13-14. Caution must be taken when splinting to ensure that it is not wrapped too tightly. If wrapped too tightly, the splint may cut off circulation below the splint. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or if the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage. Increased swelling may occur; continued monitoring of the splintered fracture is required.
13-15. When splinting, first responders or CLS should avoid—
Manipulating the fracture site too much, resulting in pain, additional damage to blood vessels, and nerves.
Securing too tightly and cutting off blood flow.
Failing to immobilize the joint above and below the fracture when possible.
Causing further injury.
Making the casualty uncomfortable during transport or evacuation.
Splinting near or over a wound that has not been properly treated.

bites.heading: If a snake bites you
lines: If a snake bites you
Seek emergency medical attention as soon as possible to start antivenom (if needed) and stop irreversible damage.
Do not drive yourself to the hospital because the snakebite can make you dizzy or pass out.
Take a photograph from a safe distance to identify the snake if possible, which may aid in faster treatment.
Keep calm.
Inform your supervisor.
Apply first aid while waiting for someone to take you to the hospital.
Lay or sit down with the bite in a neutral position of comfort.
Remove rings and watches before swelling starts.
Wash the bite with soap and water.
Cover the bite with a clean, dry dressing.
Mark the leading edge of tenderness/swelling on the skin and write the time alongside it.

bites.heading: What not to do
lines: Do not pick up the snake or try to trap it.
NEVER handle a venomous snake, not even a dead one or its decapitated head.
Do not wait for symptoms to appear; get medical help right away.
Do not apply a tourniquet, electric shock, or folk therapies.
Do not slash the wound with a knife or cut it in any way.
Do not try to suck out the venom.
Do not apply ice or immerse the wound in water.
Do not drink alcohol as a painkiller or take pain relievers (such as, aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen).

bites.heading: Insect bites and stings
lines: 16-48. First aid treatment for insect bites can vary depending on the type of insect and the individual's reaction. The general first aid steps for treating insect bites are:

Remove the stinger (if applicable): In the case of stinging insects like bees or wasps, it's important to remove the stinger as quickly as possible to prevent further venom injection. Gently scrape it off the skin using a blunt edge like a credit card or your fingernail. Avoid squeezing the venom sac, as it may release more venom.
Wash the bite area: Clean the bite site with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Be gentle and avoid excessive scrubbing.

Apply a cold compress: To alleviate pain, reduce swelling, and minimize itching, apply a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the bite area. Do this for 10-15 minutes at a time, several times a day.

Use over-the-counter remedies: Over-the-counter topical creams, ointments, or sprays containing ingredients such as hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or antihistamines can help relieve itching and inflammation. Follow the instructions and precautions on the product packaging.

Take oral antihistamines: If itching or swelling persists, you can take over-the-counter oral antihistamine to help reduce allergic reactions and relieve symptoms. Consult a pharmacist or health care professional for appropriate dosage and recommendations.
Avoid scratching: Although it may be tempting, refrain from scratching the insect bite to prevent further irritation, infection, or the development of a secondary skin condition.

Monitor for severe reactions: In rare cases, insect bites can cause severe allergic reactions, known as anaphylaxis. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, dizziness, swelling of the face or throat, or a widespread rash, seek immediate medical attention.
16-49. If the insect type is unknown or if the Service member is experiencing severe or worsening symptoms, it is best to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation and guidance.

allergic.heading: Treatment for Anaphylactic Shock
lines: 7-32. The treatment of anaphylactic shock is urgent and time sensitive. Immediate actions include calling for medical help and, if available, using the casualty’s epinephrine auto-injector. Anaphylactic reactions can manifest within seconds or minutes after exposure to an allergen, affecting the skin, respiratory, and circulatory systems.

7-33. Prompt recognition and response to anaphylactic shock are critical. Assessing both the signs and symptoms early on is essential for effective intervention. Quick and accurate identification of the condition allows for the necessary steps to be taken to mitigate its life-threatening effects.

allergic.heading: Check for Anaphylactic Shock
lines: 7-34. To effectively check for anaphylactic shock, Service members should follow a systematic approach:

Assess Symptoms: ▪ Observe for sudden and severe symptoms like difficulty breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath. ▪ Check for a rapid or weak pulse. ▪ Look for swelling of the face, lips, or tongue. ▪ Note any hives or widespread skin redness. ▪ Be alert to signs of confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness.
Ask Questions: ▪ Inquire about any known allergies or recent exposures to potential allergens. ▪ Ask if they have ingested or come into contact with a known allergen recently.
Observe Breathing: ▪ Check for signs of respiratory distress, such as rapid or labored breathing. ▪ Listen for wheezing or other abnormal breathing sounds.
Check Circulation: ▪ Assess the pulse to determine its rate and strength. ▪ Look for signs of poor circulation, such as pale or bluish skin.
Look for Other Symptoms: ▪ Be aware of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or a feeling of impending doom.

allergic.heading: Epinephrine
lines: 7-35. If anaphylactic shock is suspected, immediate medical assistance is crucial. The primary treatment involves administering epinephrine (adrenaline). If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained. Dosage guidelines are typically provided with the injector—0.15 milligrams (mg) for children and 0.3 mg for adults weighing more than 66 pounds.

7-36. Further doses of epinephrine may be necessary, administered every 5 to 10 minutes if prescribed and symptoms persist. Additionally, provide supportive measures for treating shock, respiratory failure, circulatory collapse, or cardiac arrest:
Position the casualty supine with legs elevated if injuries permit.
Perform rescue breathing and external chest compressions if required.
Monitor vital signs every three to five minutes until the casualty is stable.

poison.heading: What should I do if I think someone has been poisoned?
lines: Right away call the Poison Help line (1-800-222-1222), which connects you to your local poison center. A poison expert will tell you exactly what to do. If necessary, the poison center may stay on the phone with you while you get other help.

poison.heading: What should I do when I need to call for help?
lines: When you call the Poison Help line, be ready to give information (listed below) to the expert on the phone. It is important to stay calm. Not all medicines and household products are poisonous. Not all contact with poison results in poisoning. When you call, make sure to have the container of the product you think caused the poisoning. The label has important information. When calling the Poison Help line, be ready (if you can) to tell the expert:
The person’s age and weight
Known health conditions or problems
The product involved
How the product contacted the person (for example, by mouth, by inhaling, through the skin, or through the eyes)
How long ago the poison contacted the person
What first aid has already been given
Whether the person has vomited
Your exact location and how long it would take you to get to a hospital
If medicine has been swallowed, do not give anything by mouth until you have talked to a Poison Help expert.

poison.heading: What is the Poison Help line?
lines: The toll-free Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222. When you call the number, you will reach specially trained poison experts at a poison center that serves your area. This number provides free and confidential help 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. Interpretation services are available in 161 languages.

lost.heading: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan
lines: If you do become lost your most important tool is keeping a positive mental attitude.
Stop:
As soon as you realize you may be lost: stop, stay calm, stay put. Panic is your greatest enemy.
Think:
Go over in your mind how you got to where you are. What landmarks should you be able to see? Do not move at all until you have a specific reason to take a step.
Observe:
Get out your compass and determine the directions based on where you are standing. Do not walk aimlessly.
If you are on a trail, stay on it. All trails are marked with signs (where intersections meet) and with diamond blazers or markers. However, signs are sometimes vandalized or stolen.
As a very last resort, follow a drainage or stream downhill. This is often a difficult path but could lead to a trail or road. Again, this could be very dangerous.
Plan:
Based on your thinking and observations, come up with some possible plans, think them through then act on one of them.
If you are not very, very confident in the route, then it’s always better to stay put.
If it’s nightfall, you are injured or you are near exhaustion, stay in place.

lost.heading: If You Get Lost: self rescue, seek help
lines: 1. Attempt self rescue – Use your knowledge, skills, and tools to find your way
Stop and breath – Take a moment to calmly assess your situation
Find your location – Use your map, compass, handheld GPS, or visible landmarks to try to find your location
Retrace your steps – If it is safe to do so, retrace your steps to get back on your planned route
2. Seek help – If you cannot retrace your steps:
Call 911 – Tell them:
GPS coordinates from your phone, if available
Name of the trail or area of the park where you started your activity
Your last known location before you became lost
Description of your surroundings including visible landmarks
Types and colors of clothing you are wearing
Equipment you are carrying
Any medical conditions you may have
Stay put – Changing location will make it difficult for authorities to find you. Move only if there is an immediate threat to life
Conserve energy – Wait patiently for help to arrive and conserve your energy

lost.heading: Hug-A-Tree (for children)
lost.locator: If You Get Lost, For children
lines: 1. Hug-A-Tree
Find a tree, hug it, and stay put. If you do not see a tree around you, your “tree” can be a park bench or a big rock. The important thing is to stay in one place.

lost.heading: Shadow-Tip Methods
lines: In the first shadow-tip method, find a straight stick 1 meter long, and a level spot free of brush on which the stick will cast a definite shadow. This method is simple and accurate and consists of four steps:

Step 1. Place the stick or branch into the ground at a level spot where it will cast a distinctive shadow. Mark the shadow’s tip with a stone, twig, or other means. This first shadow mark is always west—everywhere on earth.
Step 2. Wait 10 to 15 minutes until the shadow tip moves a few centimeters. Mark the shadow tip’s new position in the same way as the first.
Step 3. Draw a straight line through the two marks to obtain an approximate east-west line.
Step 4. Stand with the first mark (west) to your left and the second mark to your right—you are now facing north. This fact is true everywhere on earth.

lost.heading: Northern Sky
lines: The main constellations to learn are the Ursa Major, also known as the Big Dipper or the Plow, and Cassiopeia (Figure 18-3). Neither of these constellations ever sets. They are always visible on a clear night. Use them to locate Polaris, also known as the polestar or the North Star. The North Star forms part of the Little Dipper handle and can be confused with the Big Dipper. Prevent confusion by using both the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia together. The Big Dipper and Cassiopeia are always directly opposite each other and rotate counterclockwise around Polaris, with Polaris in the center. The Big Dipper is a seven star constellation in the shape of a dipper. The two stars forming the outer lip of this dipper are the “pointer stars” because they point to the North Star. Mentally draw a line from the outer bottom star to the outer top star of the Big Dipper’s bucket. Extend this line about five times the distance between the pointer stars. You will find the North Star along this line. Cassiopeia has five stars that form a shape like a “W” on its side. The North Star is straight out from Cassiopeia’s center star.
After locating the North Star, locate the North Pole or true north by drawing an imaginary line directly to the earth.

lost.heading: Navigation with the Southern Cross
lines: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Southern Cross is frequently used for navigation in much the same way that Polaris is used in the Northern Hemisphere. Projecting a line from γ to α Crucis (the foot of the crucifix) about 4½ times beyond gives a point close to the Southern Celestial Pole which is also, coincidentally, where it intersects a perpendicular line taken southwards from the east–west axis of Alpha Centauri to Beta Centauri, which are stars at an alike declination to Crux and of a similar width as the cross, but higher magnitude. Argentine gauchos are documented as using Crux for night orientation in the Pampas and Patagonia.

Alpha and Beta Centauri are of similar declinations (thus distance from the pole) and are often referred as the "Southern Pointers" or just "the Pointers", allowing people to easily identify the Southern Cross, the constellation of Crux. Very few bright stars lie between Crux and the pole itself, although the constellation Musca is fairly easily recognised immediately south of Crux.

signal.heading: Signal for help
lines: Signal for help – Use the following signals to help search and rescue authorities find you:
Blow your whistle often - This will help save your energy from not yelling
Flash your flashlight – Flash the SOS pattern: Three times quickly, three times slowly, three times quickly. Use your flashlight wisely as this will drain the batteries.
Flash your mirror – This can alert planes and helicopters flying in the area
Make yourself visible – Lay out the shelter from your 10 essentials or use rocks to create a shape that can be seen by planes or helicopters flying above
Conserve energy – Wait patiently for help to arrive

signal.heading: SOS
lines: You can use lights or flags to send an SOS—three dots, three dashes, three dots. The SOS is the internationally recognized distress signal in radio Morse code. A dot is a short, sharp pulse; a dash is a longer pulse. Keep repeating the signal. When using flags, hold flags on the left side for dashes and on the right side for dots.

signal.heading: Whistles
lines: Whistles provide an excellent way for close up signaling. In some documented cases, they have been heard up to 1.6 kilometers away. Manufactured whistles have more range than a human whistle.

signal.heading: Fire
lines: During darkness, fire is the most effective visual means for signaling. Build three fires in a triangle (the international distress signal) or in a straight line with about 25 meters between the fires. Build them as soon as time and the situation permit and protect them until you need them. If you are alone, maintaining three fires may be difficult. If so, maintain one signal fire. When constructing signal fires, consider your geographic location. If in a jungle, find a natural clearing or the edge of a stream where you can build fires that the jungle foliage will not hide. You may even have to clear an area. If in a snow-covered area, you may have to clear the ground of snow or make a platform on which to build the fire so that melting snow will not extinguish it.

shelter.heading: Await rescue: find shelter, keep warm
lines: 3. Await rescue – If you do not have a phone or cell reception to call 911:
Find shelter – A place that can protect you from the elements (sun, rain, snow, etc.)
Inventory and conserve your resources – Check your 10 essentials and other items you packed to help you stay safe until help arrives
Keep warm – The temperature outside can change throughout the day. If you begin to feel cold put on any extra layers of clothing you have with you
Note: Do not build a fire if there is a high fire risk at the park or if it is wildland fire season. It could cause a wildfire and put you and others at great risk.

shelter.heading: Shelter Site Selection
lines: You must also remember the problems that could arise in your environment. For instance—
Avoid flash flood areas in foothills.
Avoid avalanche or rockslide areas in mountainous terrain.
Avoid sites near bodies of water that are below the high water mark.

shelter.heading: Basic Principles of Cold Weather Survival
lines: There are four basic principles to follow to keep warm. An easy way to remember these basic principles is to use the word COLD— C Keep clothing clean. O Avoid overheating. L Wear clothes loose and in layers. D Keep clothing dry.

shelter.heading: Poncho Lean-To
lines: To reduce heat loss to the ground, place some type of insulating material, such as leaves or pine needles, inside your lean-to.

water.heading: Consider how the water looks and how to filter it if needed
lines: Disinfection does not work as well when water is cloudy or colored. If water is cloudy, let it settle. Then filter the water through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter. Store the settled and filtered water in clean containers with covers.

water.heading: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
lines: ONLY USE WATER THAT HAS BEEN PROPERLY DISINFECTED FOR DRINKING, COOKING, MAKING ANY PREPARED DRINK, WASHING DISHES AND FOR BRUSHING TEETH.
Use bottled water or water you have properly prepared and stored as an emergency water supply.
Boil water, if you do not have bottled water. Boiling is sufficient to kill pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa (WHO, 2015).
Bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute. At altitudes above 5,000 feet (1,000 meters), boil water for three minutes.
Let water cool naturally and store it in clean containers with covers.

water.heading: Disinfect water using household bleach
lines: Disinfect water using household bleach, if you can’t boil water. Only use regular, unscented chlorine bleach products that are suitable for disinfection and sanitization as indicated on the label. The label may say that the active ingredient contains 6 or 8.25% of sodium hypochlorite. Do not use scented, color safe, or bleaches with added cleaners.
Locate a clean dropper from your medicine cabinet or emergency supply kit.
Locate a fresh liquid chlorine bleach or liquid chlorine bleach that is stored at room temperatures for less than one year.

Use the table below as a guide to decide the amount of bleach you should add to the water, for example, 8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, to each gallon of water. Double the amount of bleach if the water is cloudy, colored, or very cold.
Stir and let stand for 30 minutes. The water should have a slight chlorine odor. If it doesn’t, repeat the dosage and let stand for another 15 minutes before use.
If the chlorine taste is too strong, pour the water from one clean container to another and let it stand for a few hours before use.

water.heading: Water Filtration Devices
lines: If the water you find is also muddy, stagnant, and foul smelling, you can clear the water—
By placing it in a container and letting it stand for 12 hours.
By pouring it through a filtering system. Note: These procedures only clear the water and make it more palatable. You will have to purify it.

water.heading: Water Procurement
lines: Water is one of your most urgent needs in a survival situation. You can‘t live long without it, especially in hot areas where you lose water rapidly through perspiration. Even in cold areas, you need a minimum of 2 liters of water each day to maintain efficiency. More than three-fourths of your body is composed of fluids. Your body loses fluid as a result of heat, cold, stress, and exertion. To function effectively, you must replace the fluid your body loses. So, one of your first goals is to obtain an adequate supply of water.

food.heading: Food Safety and Sanitation
lines: Without electricity or a cold source food stored in refrigerators and freezers can become unsafe. Bacteria in food grow rapidly at temperatures between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit and if these foods are consumed you can become very sick. Thawed food usually can be eaten if it is still “refrigerator cold.” It can be re-frozen if it still contains ice crystals. Remember “When in doubt, throw it out.”
Do:
Keep food in covered containers.
Keep cooking and eating utensils clean.
Throw away any food that has come into contact with contaminated flood water.
Throw away any food that has been at room temperature for two hours or more.
Throw away any food that has an unusual odor, color or texture.
Use ready-to-feed formula. If you must mix infant formula use bottled water or boiled water as a last resort.
Don’t:
Eat foods from cans that are swollen, dented or corroded, even though the product may look safe to eat.
Eat any food that looks or smells abnormal, even if the can looks normal.
Let garbage accumulate inside, both for fire and sanitation reasons.

flood.heading: During a Flood
lines: Evacuate immediately, if told to do so. Never drive around barricades. Local responders use them to safely direct traffic out of flooded areas.

Contact your healthcare provider if you are sick and need medical attention. Wait for further care instructions and shelter in place, if possible. If you are experiencing a medical emergency, call 9-1-1.
Listen to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio or local alerting systems for current emergency information and instructions regarding flooding.
Do not walk, swim or drive through flood waters. Turn Around. Don’t Drown!
Stay off bridges over fast-moving water. Fast-moving water can wash bridges away without warning.
Stay inside your car if it is trapped in rapidly moving water. Get on the roof if water is rising inside the car.
Get to the highest level if trapped in a building. Only get on the roof if necessary and once there, signal for help. Do not climb into a closed attic to avoid getting trapped by rising floodwater.

flood.heading: After a Flood: electricity and water
lines: Be aware of the risk of electrocution. Do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Turn off the electricity to prevent electric shock if it is safe to do so.
Avoid wading in floodwater, which can be contaminated and contain dangerous debris. Underground or downed power lines can electrically charge the water.

flood.heading: After a Flood
lines: Pay attention to authorities for information and instructions. Return home only when authorities say it is safe.
Avoid driving except in emergencies.
Wear heavy work gloves, protective clothing and boots during cleanup and use appropriate face coverings or masks if cleaning mold or other debris.

People with asthma and other lung conditions and/or immune suppression should not enter buildings with indoor water leaks or mold growth that can be seen or smelled. Children should not take part in disaster cleanup work.
Be aware that snakes and other animals may be in your house.
Be aware of the risk of electrocution. Do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Turn off the electricity to prevent electric shock if it is safe to do so.
Avoid wading in floodwater, which can be contaminated and contain dangerous debris. Underground or downed power lines can electrically charge the water.
Use a generator or other gasoline-powered machinery ONLY outdoors and away from windows.

earthquake.heading: Protect Yourself During Earthquakes
lines: 1. Drop (or Lock)
Drop where you are onto hands and knees.
2. Cover

Cover your head and neck with one arm and hand. If a sturdy table or desk is nearby, crawl underneath it for shelter. If no shelter is nearby, crawl next to an interior wall (away from windows). Stay on your knees; bend over to protect vital organs.
3. Hold On

Hold until the shaking stops. If under shelter, hold on with one hand and be ready to move with it when the shelter moves. If not under shelter, hold on to your head and neck with both arms and hands.
Using a Cane?
If you use a cane: DROP, COVER, and HOLD ON or sit on a chair, bed, etc. and cover your head and neck with both hands. Keep your cane near you so it can be used when the shaking stops.
Using a Walker or Wheelchair?

If you use a walker or wheelchair: LOCK your wheels (if applicable). If using a walker carefully get as low as possible. Bend over and COVER your head/neck with your arms, a book, or a pillow. Then HOLD ON until the shaking stops.

earthquake.heading: After an Earthquake: first
lines: There can be serious hazards after an earthquake, such as damage to the building, leaking gas and water lines or downed power lines.
Expect aftershocks to follow the main shock of an earthquake. Be ready to Drop, Cover and Hold On if you feel an aftershock.
If you are in a damaged building, go outside and quickly move away from the building. Do not enter damaged buildings.
If you are trapped, send a text or bang on a pipe or wall. Cover your mouth with your shirt for protection and instead of shouting, use a whistle.
If you are in an area that may experience tsunamis, go inland or to higher ground immediately after the shaking stops. Avoid contact with floodwaters as they can contain chemicals, sewage and debris.
Check yourself to see if you are hurt and help others if you have training. Be the help until help arrives.

earthquake.heading: After an Earthquake: then
lines: If you are sick or injured and need medical attention, contact your healthcare provider for instructions. If you are experiencing a medical emergency, call 9-1-1.
Once you are safe, pay attention to local news reports for emergency information and instructions via battery-operated radio, TV, social media or from cell phone text alerts.
Use social media to let people know you’re okay.
Use text messages to communicate. This may be more reliable than phone calls and can save batter power.

Be careful when cleaning up. Wear protective clothing, including a long-sleeved shirt, long pants, work gloves and sturdy thick-soled shoes. Do not try to remove heavy debris by yourself. Use an appropriate mask if cleaning mold or other debris. People with asthma and other lung conditions and/or immune suppression should not enter buildings with indoor water leaks or mold growth that can be seen or smelled. Children should not take part in disaster cleanup work.

wildfire.heading: Stay Safe During
lines: Pay attention to emergency alerts and notifications for information and instructions.
Evacuate immediately if authorities tell you to do so.

Check with local authorities for the latest information about public shelters or check open locations on the FEMA app. You can also download the free Red Cross Emergency app for a list of open Red Cross shelters in your area.
Consider making plans with friends or family to shelter with them where you may be safer and more comfortable.
If trapped, call 9-1-1 and give your location, but be aware that emergency response could be delayed or impossible. Turn on lights to help rescuers find you.

wildfire.heading: Smoke
lines: Use an N95 mask to protect yourself from smoke inhalation or limit your exposure to smoke by doing the following:
Choose a room to close off from outside air and set up a portable air cleaner or filter to keep the air in this room clean even when it’s smoky in the rest of the building and outdoors.

Use high efficiency filters in your central air conditioning system to capture fine particles from smoke. If your system has fresh air intake, set the system to “recirculate” mode and close the outdoor intake damper.
If you are not ordered to evacuate but smoky conditions exist, stay inside in a safe location or go to a community building where smoke levels are lower.
If you are sick and need medical attention, contact your healthcare provider for further care instructions and shelter in place, if possible.

wildfire.heading: Returning Home After a Wildfire
lines: Do not return home until authorities say it is safe to do so.
Avoid hot ash, charred trees, smoldering debris and live embers. The ground may contain heat pockets that can burn you or spark another fire.
When cleaning, wear protective clothing – including a long-sleeved shirt, long pants, work gloves and sturdy thick-soled shoes – during clean-up efforts.

Use a respirator to limit your exposure, and wet debris to minimize breathing dust particles. People with asthma, COPD and/or other lung conditions should take precautions in areas with poor air quality, as it can worsen symptoms.
Document property damage with photographs. Conduct an inventory and contact your insurance company for assistance.
Send text messages or use social media to reach out to family and friends. Phone systems are often busy following a disaster. Make calls only in emergencies.

storm.heading: If You Are Under A Tornado or Severe Weather Warning
lines: Listen to local weather reports and officials for updated emergency information. Follow their instructions to remain safe.
Go to a public shelter if you can't stay at home.
Stay away from windows, doors, and outside walls.
Use your arms to protect your head and neck.
Watch out for flying debris that can cause injury or death.

storm.heading: Before a Tornado: a safe shelter
lines: Identify and practice going to a safe shelter such as a safe room built using FEMA criteria or a storm shelter built to ICC 500 standards. The next best protection is a small, interior, windowless room or basement on the lowest level of a sturdy building.

storm.heading: During a Tornado
lines: Immediately go to a safe location that you have identified.
Pay attention to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio, or local alerting systems for current emergency information and instructions.
Protect yourself by covering your head or neck with your arms and putting materials such as furniture and blankets around or on top of you.
In a car or truck: There is no safe option when caught in a tornado in a car, just slightly less dangerous ones.
If the tornado is visible, far away, and the traffic is light, you may be able to drive out of its path by moving at right angles to the tornado.
If you are caught by extreme winds or flying debris, park the car as quickly and safely as possible -- out of the traffic lanes.
Stay in the car with the seat belt on. Put your head down below the windows; cover your head with your hands and a blanket, coat, or other cushion if possible.
If you can safely get noticeably lower than the level of the roadway, leave your car and lie in that area, covering your head with your hands.
Avoid seeking shelter under bridges, which can create deadly traffic hazards while offering little protection against flying debris.

storm.heading: Stay Safe During Thunderstorms & Lightning
lines: If you are under a thunderstorm warning:
When thunder roars, go indoors! Move from outdoors into a building or car with a roof.
Pay attention to alerts and warnings.
Avoid using electronic devices connected to an electrical outlet.
Avoid running water.
Turn Around. Don’t Drown! Do not drive through flooded roadways. Just six inches of fast-moving water can knock you down, and one foot of moving water can sweep your vehicle away.

storm.heading: During a Hurricane/Typhoon
lines: Stay Informed
Pay attention to emergency information and alerts.
If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and local officials tell you to evacuate, do so immediately.
Dealing with the Weather
Determine how best to protect yourself from high winds and flooding.
Take refuge in a designated storm shelter or an interior room for high winds.
Go to the highest level of the building if you are trapped by flooding. Do not climb into a closed attic. You may become trapped by rising flood water.
Do not walk, swim or drive through flood waters. Turn Around. Don’t Drown! Just six inches of fast-moving water can knock you down, and one foot of moving water can sweep your vehicle away.

power_out.heading: Generator Safety
lines: Generators can be helpful when the power goes out. It is important to know how use them safely to prevent carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and other hazards.
Generators and fuel should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows, doors and attached garages.
Install working carbon monoxide detectors on every level of your home. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that can kill you, your family and pets.
Keep the generator dry and protected from rain or flooding. Touching a wet generator or devices connected to one can cause electrical shock.
Always connect the generator to appliances with heavy-duty extension cords.
Let the generator cool before refueling. Fuel spilled on hot engine parts can ignite.
Follow manufacturer’s instructions carefully.

power_out.heading: Power Outage Tips
lines: Keep freezers and refrigerators closed.
Use a generator, but ONLY outdoors and away from windows.

Do not use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It increases your risk of carbon monoxide poisoning. Using an oven or stovetop can also increase the risk of fires, burns and could damage the appliance.
Disconnect appliances and electronics to avoid damage from electrical surges.
Have alternate plans for refrigerating medicines or using power-dependent medical devices.
Check with local officials about heating and cooling locations open near you.

power_out.heading: Food Storage
lines: Have enough nonperishable food and water. Keep freezers and refrigerators closed. The refrigerator will keep food cold for about four hours. A full freezer will keep the temperature for about 48 hours. Use coolers with ice if necessary. Monitor temperatures with a thermometer. Throw out food if the temperature is 40 degrees or higher.

power_out.heading: Returning After A Power Outage
lines: When in doubt, throw it out! Throw away any food that has been exposed to temperatures 40 degrees or higher for two hours or more, or that has an unusual odor, color or texture.
If the power is out for more than a day, discard any medication that should be refrigerated, unless the drug’s label says otherwise. Consult your doctor or pharmacist immediately for a new supply.

carbon_monoxide.heading: Symptoms
lines: The most common symptoms of CO poisoning are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. CO symptoms are often described as “flu-like.”
If you breathe in a lot of CO, it can make you pass out or kill you. People who are sleeping, drunk, or under the influence of other substances can die from CO poisoning before they have symptoms.

carbon_monoxide.heading: Portable generators
lines: Operate your generator outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors, and vents to avoid CO poisoning
Never use a generator inside your home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.
Only use generators outside, more than 20 feet away from any windows, doors, and vents.
When using a generator, use a battery-powered or battery backup CO detector in your home.
If you have a had a poisoning incident related to any generator...

carbon_monoxide.heading: Chimneys, charcoal, and portable appliances
lines: Have your chimney checked or cleaned every year. Chimneys can be blocked by debris, which can cause CO to build up inside your home or cabin.
Never burn charcoal indoors. Burning charcoal - red, gray, black, or white - gives off CO.
Never use a portable gas camp stove indoors.
Do not use portable flameless chemical heaters indoors.
